Why Async Python Scales So Well

By Jane Doe, March 3, 2026

Traditional synchronous web servers block an entire operating system thread every time they wait for a network socket or a database query to return, which puts a hard ceiling on how many users a single machine can serve at once.

By contrast, an event loop driven by Uvicorn and FastAPI can juggle thousands of waiting HTTP connections on a single CPU core, switching between tasks whenever input or output is pending, so the processor almost never sits idle while the network catches up.

A tiny example

The snippet below starts three slow downloads at the same time instead of one after another, and the whole batch finishes in roughly the time of the slowest request.

import asyncio
import httpx

async def main():
    async with httpx.AsyncClient() as client:
        pages = await asyncio.gather(*(client.get(u) for u in URLS))

How much faster is it?

In our own benchmark on a modest laptop, the difference was dramatic once the number of concurrent clients climbed past a few hundred.

Server modelRequests per second
Threaded sync900
Async event loop12000

The lesson is not that async is magic, but that most web workloads spend their lives waiting, and a design that embraces waiting wins. Dr. Smith summed it up neatly at last year's conference: concurrency is about structure, while parallelism is about execution.
